meta.title: Indian Ex-Servicemen PTSD Navigator - MVP Data Layer
meta.disclaimer: This tool provides educational information only. It is not legal or medical advice. Always verify with a Veteran Service Officer, a lawyer, or the relevant government office before acting. Source citations are provided for every rule so they can be independently verified.

crisis_resource.name: Vandrevala Foundation Helpline (24/7 mental health crisis support, India)
crisis_resource.note: Always displayed on every screen of the app, not just this data note.

sources: Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare (desw.gov.in) - Pension Regulations & Casualty Pension Award pages
Entitlement Rules for Casualty Pensionary Awards, 2008
Supreme Court of India judgments (via official reporting and legal aggregators)

intake_questions.prompt: How many years did you serve?
What year were you discharged? (leave blank if still serving)
Are you currently enrolled in ECHS (Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme)?
When did your symptoms (nightmares, flashbacks, hypervigilance, etc.) start?
Have you already been through a Medical Board or filed a disability pension claim?
options: Medical Board found it attributable / aggravated
Medical Board rejected as 'not attributable' or 'constitutional' or 'lifestyle related'

intake_questions.prompt: In your own words, describe what happened and how you've been feeling. Include any specific incidents, dates, or witnesses if you remember them.
intake_questions.note: This field is passed to an LLM extraction step to pull out structured facts (incident dates, unit/posting, witnesses, symptom description) - NOT used to make legal determinations.

eligibility_rules.condition: discharge_status in ['Discharged - normal completion of service', 'Discharged/Invalided on medical grounds'] AND receiving_any_pension == true

result.plain_language: As a pensioner ex-serviceman, you and your dependents are generally eligible to enroll in ECHS for healthcare including mental health support, regardless of whether your PTSD claim has been decided.
result.source: ECHS Handbook, Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare (desw.gov.in)

result.plain_language: Regulation 173 of the Pension Regulations for the Army, 1961 allows disability pension where a disability is attributable to or aggravated by military service and assessed at 20% or above.
result.source: Pension Regulations for the Army, 1961, Regulation 173

eligibility_rules.condition: medical_board_status in ['Medical Board rejected as \'not attributable\' or \'constitutional\' or \'lifestyle related\'', 'Claim rejected by PCDA(Pension)', 'Already appealed and rejected again']

result.eligible_for: Grounds for appeal - presumption of soundness
result.plain_language: A member of the Armed Forces is presumed to have been in sound physical and mental condition at the time of entering service, unless a disability was specifically noted or recorded at entry. If nothing was noted on your entry medical exam, this presumption may work in your favor.
result.source: Dharamvir Singh v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 2013 (8 SCR 1119)

eligibility_rules.condition: medical_board_status in ['Medical Board rejected as \'not attributable\' or \'constitutional\' or \'lifestyle related\'']

result.plain_language: Courts have ruled that a bare statement from a Medical Board that a disability is 'constitutional,' 'lifestyle related,' or 'not attributable to service' -- without individualized reasons explaining why -- is not enough to lawfully deny a disability pension. If your rejection letter does not explain the specific reasoning behind the conclusion, this may be a valid ground for appeal.
result.source: Delhi High Court ruling on 'lifestyle disorder' denials (2026); Supreme Court ruling on unreasoned Medical Board reports in discharge/pension denial case

eligibility_rules.condition: medical_board_status == 'Claim rejected by PCDA(Pension)' AND board_opinion_was_favorable == true

result.eligible_for: Grounds for appeal - authority overriding Medical Board
result.plain_language: If your Medical Board found your condition attributable to or aggravated by military service, but a separate administrative authority (like PCDA Pension) rejected your claim anyway, this override has been challenged in tribunals. Whether an administrative authority can lawfully overrule a duly constituted Medical Board's opinion is a live legal question you should raise on appeal.
result.source: Union of India v. Rajbir Singh, Supreme Court; Armed Forces Tribunal case law

result.plain_language: You haven't started the formal process yet. Your first step is typically a medical examination/Medical Board assessment. Before that, it can help to gather any documentation of incidents, dates, postings, and witnesses that connect your symptoms to your service.
result.source: General process guidance, Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare

not_started: Gather service records (posting history, deployment/operation details)
Write down specific incidents with approximate dates, even if memory is imperfect
Note names of anyone who witnessed events or noticed changes in you
Request a medical examination / Medical Board assessment through your unit or the relevant Command Hospital
Consider enrolling in ECHS now if not already enrolled - you don't need a decided claim to access ECHS mental health care
rejected_unreasoned: Request a copy of the full Medical Board proceedings, not just the rejection letter
Check whether the rejection gives individualized reasons or just a general label ('constitutional', 'lifestyle related')
If reasons are missing or generic, cite the precedent on individualized reasoning in your appeal
File your statutory appeal within the required timeframe (verify current deadline with a Veteran Service Officer or lawyer, as these can change)
Consider approaching the Armed Forces Tribunal if statutory appeals are exhausted
already_appealed: Consult a lawyer experienced in Armed Forces Tribunal matters - many veteran advocacy groups provide free or low-cost referrals
Review whether the presumption-of-soundness argument was raised in your prior appeals
Gather any new medical evidence connecting your condition to service, if available
File before the Armed Forces Tribunal if you haven't already

legal_precedent_library.case_name: Dharamvir Singh v. Union of India
legal_precedent_library.plain_summary: A soldier discharged for epilepsy was denied disability pension. The Supreme Court held that a member of the Armed Forces is presumed to be in sound physical and mental condition upon entering service, unless a disability was noted or recorded at the time of entry. This presumption favors the veteran unless the government can show otherwise.
legal_precedent_library.relevance: Useful if nothing was noted about a mental health condition on your entry medical exam.

legal_precedent_library.case_name: Union of India v. Rajbir Singh
legal_precedent_library.plain_summary: The Court examined whether a Medical Board's opinion that a disability was 'not attributable to or aggravated by' service was, by itself, enough to deny a pension. It clarified how Pension Regulation 173 should be interpreted and applied.
legal_precedent_library.relevance: Useful for understanding how much weight a Medical Board's bare opinion should carry.

legal_precedent_library.case_name: Rajumon T.M. v. Union of India
legal_precedent_library.plain_summary: A sepoy discharged for schizophrenia after 9+ years of service was denied pension based on a Medical Board finding of 'constitutional' disability with no stated reasons. The Supreme Court held that discharge or pension denial based on an unreasoned Medical Board report is unsustainable in law.
legal_precedent_library.relevance: Directly useful if your rejection letter doesn't explain its reasoning.

legal_precedent_library.case_name: Delhi High Court ruling on 'lifestyle disorder' denial
legal_precedent_library.citation: Delhi High Court, 2026 (affirming Armed Forces Tribunal order)
legal_precedent_library.plain_summary: An Air Force veteran's disability pension was initially denied on the basis that his conditions were 'lifestyle related' rather than service-connected. The Court held that a bald statement of 'lifestyle disorder' or 'not attributable,' without individualized reasoning, is insufficient to deny a pension.
legal_precedent_library.relevance: Useful precedent if your rejection uses generic labels like 'lifestyle disorder' without explanation.
